I am 56 years old and have been farming in Quzhou County my whole life. My family has about 8 mu of good flat land near the village, and I know every inch of it. I went to middle school, which was more than enough to understand what the extension agents tell us and to read the fertilizer bags. At my age, I do not take big risks. The wheat-maize rotation has fed my family for generations, and with grain prices stable and the local grain station reliable, I see no reason to change.

Last October I sowed my winter wheat. I used an improved variety that my neighbors have had success with — not the old traditional seeds, because the yield is too low, but not some fancy new thing either. I prepared the land with rotary tillage and put down basal compound fertilizer. Now it is spring, the wheat is greening up after winter dormancy, and my job is to manage it through to the June harvest. I will topdress with nitrogen at the jointing stage, irrigate three or four times depending on rainfall, and spray for insects, weeds, and fungus as needed. I have a well, so water is available, but electricity costs money so I do not waste it.

After the wheat harvest in early June, I will immediately plant summer maize. I always use hybrid maize seed — everyone does, because the yield difference is huge. I will plant directly into the wheat stubble with no tillage to save time, fuel, and labor. Maize grows fast in the summer heat. I will irrigate twice, usually at the jointing and filling stages, and spray for insects and weeds two or three times. By late September or early October the maize will be dry and ready to harvest.

I thought about planting a couple of mu of cotton or vegetables like some of the younger farmers do, but the market is uncertain and my wife and I are getting older. We will stick to grain. It is safe, the machines can do most of the work, and we know exactly what to expect.
